title: How LEFT JOIN Quietly Turns Your Matches into NULLs — and How to Stop It
course: Why LEFT JOIN Can Quietly Turn Your Matches into NULLs

events.narration: Hey, welcome in. This lesson's for you if you've been writing LEFT JOINs for a few months, you're pretty comfortable with the syntax, but every now and then you get NULLs in your results that just don't make sense. You checked the data, the keys exist, the rows are there, and yet, NULLs. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to spot three hidden causes of those phantom NULLs and fix each one on the spot. Let's dig in.

Here's our schema. Two tables, nice and simple. We've got a customers table with customer ID, customer name, and region. And we've got an orders table with order ID, customer ID, order date, and amount. The kind of setup you'd see in any reporting database. Nothing weird, nothing exotic. That's what makes the NULLs so frustrating, because this looks like it should just work.

Alright, here's our baseline query. We're doing a straightforward LEFT JOIN from orders over to customers on customer ID. We're pulling back order ID, customer ID, customer name, region, and amount. This is the query you'd write on day one of building an orders report. Let's run it and see what comes back.

Okay, eleven rows back. And right away, look at order ID eight, customer ID is NULL, customer name is NULL, region is NULL, but the amount is five hundred twenty point zero zero. There's a real order sitting there with no customer attached. Same story with order ID ten, amount sixty-four point eight zero, completely orphaned. And then there's order ID nine, this one's interesting, it has customer ID nine hundred ninety-nine, but customer name and region are both NULL. So that customer ID exists in orders but doesn't match anything in the customers table. Three different rows, three different flavors of NULL. Most of the other rows look fine. Bright Elm Bakery shows up twice, order IDs one and six, amounts two hundred forty-nine point five zero and three hundred ten point six zero. Copper Fox Brewing also appears twice. Everything's matching beautifully, except for those three problem rows. And here's the thing, this isn't a missing data problem. This is a join behavior problem. There are three specific traps that cause this, and we're going to break each one open.

Trap number one, and this one's a classic. We've got the same LEFT JOIN, but now we've added a WHERE clause filtering on region equals Northeast. Region lives on the customers table, that's the right side of our join. Seems reasonable, right? You just want Northeast orders. But watch what happens.

Three rows. That's it. We went from eleven rows down to three. Order ID one, Bright Elm Bakery, two hundred forty-nine point five zero. Order ID five, Finch and Fern Café, one thousand three hundred forty point zero zero. Order ID six, Bright Elm Bakery again, three hundred ten point six zero. Every other order just vanished. Not turned into NULLs, completely gone. Your LEFT JOIN silently became an INNER JOIN. Here's why. When the LEFT JOIN can't find a match, it fills the right-side columns with NULL. Then the WHERE clause comes along and asks, "is region equal to Northeast?" Well, NULL isn't equal to anything. That comparison returns UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN gets filtered out. So every unmatched row, plus every row where region isn't Northeast, gets dropped. Your LEFT JOIN did its job. The WHERE clause undid it.

Here's the fix. Same filter, region equals Northeast, but we've moved it into the ON clause. This tells S-Q-L, "when you're looking for matches, only consider customers in the Northeast. But if there's no match, still keep the left-side row." Let's see the difference.

Now we're talking. All eleven rows are back. The Northeast customers, Bright Elm Bakery and Finch and Fern Café, still have their names and regions filled in. But look at order ID two, Copper Fox Brewing is a Midwest customer, so customer name and region come back as NULL because the ON clause filter didn't match. The row survived though. Same with order ID three, four, seven, and the rest. Every single order is preserved. The non-Northeast ones just have NULLs on the right side, which is exactly what a LEFT JOIN is supposed to do. That's the fix. Right-table filters go in the ON clause, not the WHERE clause.
And just to drive the point home, here's a side-by-side revenue comparison. We're summing the amount column and counting rows for both approaches. Let's see how bad the damage actually is.

Wow. The broken WHERE approach gives us total revenue of one thousand nine hundred point one zero with only three rows. The fixed ON clause approach? Three thousand eight hundred fifty-seven point one five across all eleven rows. That's almost two thousand dollars in revenue that just disappeared from your report because of where you put a filter. Imagine handing that broken number to a stakeholder. That's not a rounding error, that's half your data missing.

Now let's talk about trap number two, duplicate keys. Let's go back to our baseline result. Remember how Bright Elm Bakery appeared in two rows? That's fine, those are two different orders, order IDs one and six. But imagine the customers table had a duplicate row for that same customer ID. Your LEFT JOIN would cross every matching order with every matching customer row, doubling those rows silently. You wouldn't get an error. You'd just get inflated counts and wrong totals downstream. The defense? Before you join, run a GROUP BY on your join key with a HAVING COUNT greater than one. If anything comes back, you've got duplicates to clean up first.

Trap number three, and this one's the sneakiest. Look at order IDs eight and ten. Their customer ID is NULL. Now, even if the customers table also had a row where customer ID was NULL, the join still wouldn't match them. Because in S-Q-L, NULL doesn't equal NULL. That comparison returns UNKNOWN, not TRUE. So the LEFT JOIN keeps those left-side rows, fills the right side with NULLs, and you're staring at what looks like missing data when really the data's there, it just can't match on a NULL key. The fix? Use COALESCE to replace NULLs with a sentinel value before joining, or if your database supports it, use IS NOT DISTINCT FROM instead of equals in your ON clause. Either way, you're telling S-Q-L that two NULLs should be treated as a match.

Alright, here's your diagnostic checklist. Before you trust any LEFT JOIN result, ask three questions. One, are any right-table filters sitting in the WHERE clause? Move them to ON. Two, does the right table have duplicate keys? Run a GROUP BY HAVING COUNT check. Three, do your join key columns contain NULLs? Handle them with COALESCE. And honestly, just make it a habit, run a row count before and after every LEFT JOIN. If the numbers don't make sense, one of these three traps is almost certainly why. In the next lesson, we'll build reusable CTE patterns that catch these problems automatically, before your stakeholders do. See you there.
